source: Mintzberg (1978) Patterns in Strategy Formation, Management Science 24(9):934-948 (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Founding paper. Defines strategy as a pattern in a stream of decisions, so researchers can study strategies that were intended and strategies that were realized despite intention. Argues the usual definition makes strategies look like deliberate plans conceived ahead of decisions, which is an ex post illusion. Reviews two completed studies.
numbers: Cases: Volkswagenwerk 1934 to 1974 and the US government in Vietnam 1950 to 1973. Crossref lists 2,354 citing works.
quote: By defining a strategy as 'a pattern in a stream of decisions,' we are able to research strategy formation in a broad descriptive context.
limits: Case studies, not experiments. Only the abstract was opened; the case detail and any numbers in the body were not read.
agent_relevance: Treat the agent's policy as the realized pattern across its steps, and the written plan as only the intended part. Log both so S9 can compare them.

source: Mintzberg (1978) Patterns in Strategy Formation: three conclusions (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Three themes: strategy formation is the interplay of a dynamic environment and bureaucratic momentum, with leadership mediating; strategies follow life cycles and change-continuity cycles; and the gap between intended and realized strategy is the heart of the process.
numbers: Themes drawn from the Volkswagen (1934-1974) and Vietnam (1950-1973) studies. No effect sizes.
limits: Qualitative inference from two cases. The cycles claim is not tested statistically in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Momentum plus environment gives a model of when a scaffold should hold course (momentum) and when it should break pattern (a signal from outside). Fits guardrail G1: change course only on a signal.

source: Mintzberg and Waters (1985) Of strategies, deliberate and emergent, SMJ 6(3):257-272 (abstract via Crossref and IDEAS/RePEc)
finding: Deliberate and emergent strategy are two ends of a continuum, not a dichotomy. Real strategies lie between. The paper lists eight types found in research: planned, entrepreneurial, ideological, umbrella, process, unconnected, consensus, imposed.
numbers: Crossref lists 3,027 citing works; IDEAS shows 407. Crossref reference list length: 21. Eight types named.
quote: Deliberate and emergent strategies may be conceived as two ends of a continuum along which real-world strategies lie.
limits: Only the abstract was opened (full text paywalled; a Scribd copy returned no text). Type definitions elsewhere in this file are from memory and flagged opened:false.
agent_relevance: The agent's plan quality should be a position on a continuum, with a dial for how much is fixed ahead. Not a binary plan-vs-react switch.

source: Mintzberg and Waters (1985) core vocabulary: intended, deliberate, unrealized, emergent, realized (recalled, full text not opened)
finding: Recalled definition, to be verified against the full text. Intended strategy that is realized is deliberate. Intended strategy that is not realized is unrealized. A realized pattern that was never intended is emergent. Realized = deliberate + emergent. A perfectly deliberate strategy needs precise intentions, shared by the organization, realized as intended despite the environment. A perfectly emergent one needs consistency in action with no intention.
numbers: No numbers in the vocabulary. Wikipedia 'Strategic management' (opened) confirms the term emergent is used for a realized pattern that differs from intent.
limits: Memory only. Do not quote it as verified. By recollection the paper calls both pure forms implausible.
agent_relevance: This gives a ready measure for S9: share of the final solution path that was in the first plan (deliberate) versus added during the run (emergent), and which planned steps were dropped (unrealized).

source: Mintzberg and Waters (1985) type examples: umbrella, process, imposed, National Film Board, Steinberg (recalled, not opened)
finding: Recalled: umbrella strategy means leaders set broad targets and let others fill details. Process strategy means leaders control process and structure, not content. Imposed strategy comes from the environment. Cases in the research series include the Canadian National Film Board and Steinberg Inc. Details and dates were not checked.
numbers: No verified figures.
limits: Memory only. Case names beyond Volkswagen and Vietnam (confirmed in the 1978 abstract) are not verified.
agent_relevance: Umbrella and process strategy map to a scaffold where the program fixes states and budgets but the model fills content. Matches section 1 of the schema (program decides transitions, model fills slots).

source: Mintzberg (1990) The design school: reconsidering the basic premises of strategic management, SMJ 11(3):171-195 (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Critiques the design school (fit between external threat and opportunity and internal distinctive competence). Its premises: conscious control by the chief executive, a simple informal model, unique explicit simple strategies, fully formulated before implementation. The critique targets conscious assessment of strengths and weaknesses, the need for explicit strategies, and the split between formulation and implementation.
numbers: Crossref lists 911 citing works, 84 references.
quote: it calls into question some of the most deep-seated beliefs in the field of strategic management
limits: Argument paper, not empirical. Mintzberg is a party to the dispute. Page range is from memory.
agent_relevance: The split between formulation and implementation is what our scaffold does by design (plan state, then act state). The critique says to expect a cost when they are cut apart. S9 closes the loop to reduce it.

source: Ansoff (1991) Critique of Henry Mintzberg's 'The design school', SMJ 12(6):449-461 (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Planning-school side of the dispute. Ansoff judges Mintzberg's critique deficient on method and on fact, and says Mintzberg's own principles are at odds with observed practice. He blames a definition of strategy at odds with practice, mixing prescriptive and descriptive claims, and not defining context.
numbers: Crossref lists 373 citing works.
limits: Combatant in the debate; no data in the abstract. Page range is from memory.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: the planning school says context decides which approach wins. Test our agent by task type, not once for all.

source: Mintzberg (1991) Learning 1, planning 0: reply to Igor Ansoff, SMJ 12(6) (metadata via Crossref)
finding: Mintzberg's reply in the same issue. Only the title and metadata were opened; no abstract is deposited.
numbers: Crossref lists 208 citing works.
limits: Content not read. Listed so the debate chain is complete: 1990 critique, 1991 Ansoff, 1991 reply. Note it is a reply to Ansoff, not to Goold.
agent_relevance: None beyond marking the debate as argued in prose, not settled by data.

source: Burgelman (1983) A process model of internal corporate venturing in the diversified major firm, ASQ 28:223 (metadata via Crossref)
finding: Field study of strategy made below the top. Only metadata was opened; the study design (single large firm, venture cases) is recalled, not read.
numbers: Crossref lists 1,557 citing works. Case count and firm not verified.
limits: Single firm. Content not read.
agent_relevance: Source of the idea that useful new strategy can start at the edge and be selected later by management.

source: Burgelman (1991) Intraorganizational ecology of strategy making and organizational adaptation, Organization Science 2(3):239 (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Conceptual model of emergence. Two processes: induced (top-down, fits current strategy) and autonomous (bottom-up, new initiatives). Internal selection combines with external selection. Field data come from the evolution of Intel's corporate strategy. Proposes that consistently successful firms run both at once, and that successful reorientations were preceded by internal experimentation and selection through the autonomous process.
numbers: Crossref lists 1,047 citing works. One firm (Intel). No effect sizes.
quote: successful reorientations in organizations are likely to have been preceded by internal experimentation and selection processes effected through the autonomous process.
limits: One case; propositions are not tested statistically. Survivorship risk because the firm studied survived.
agent_relevance: Template for S9: keep an induced path (follow the plan) and an autonomous path (cheap side attempts), with code-run selection. Supports operator use on a signal, not on a timer.

source: Mintzberg's fall-of-planning argument (1994), as summarised on Wikipedia 'Strategic planning' (opened)
finding: Mintzberg: strategy formation is creative synthesis ('connecting the dots'), not systematisable. Planning is analysis ('finding the dots'): it coordinates and measures but works around strategy formation, not inside it. Plans mainly communicate intentions, align the organisation and win outside support. Managers cannot take charge of strategy through a formalised process.
numbers: No numbers. The same page notes the 2019 George, Walker and Monster meta-analysis of almost 9,000 organisations found a positive planning effect, strongest on goal achievement; McKinsey 2006 survey found planning not used for the most important decisions.
limits: Secondary summary; the page names the 1994 article 'The Fall and Rise of Strategic Planning' (the book is 'The Rise and Fall'). Opposing meta-analytic evidence exists (see subfield 04).
agent_relevance: Planning as analysis and formation as synthesis maps onto: code does the analysis (counting, checks), the model does the synthesis (reframing). Matches 'program decides, model fills'.

source: Wikipedia 'Strategic management' (part 1, opened): Mintzberg definitions and Chaffee's models
finding: Secondary summary. Mintzberg 1988: five types of strategy including strategy as pattern; a realized pattern that differs from intent is emergent. 1994: strategic thinking is synthesis, 'connecting the dots'. Chaffee (1985): three models of strategy, linear, adaptive, interpretive; strategy may be planned (intended) or unplanned (emergent). Mintzberg grouped strategy into 10 schools in three categories.
numbers: 10 schools; 3 categories; 5 types; Chaffee 3 models.
limits: Wikipedia; dates and attributions differ from the primary literature (the five Ps are from 1987). Not independently verified.
agent_relevance: Chaffee's adaptive model (shrink the planning window) is the closest human analogue to ReAct-style agents.

source: Wikipedia 'Strategic management' (part 2, opened): Moncrieff, Markides, Isenberg, Bolisani
finding: Moncrieff (1999): strategy is partly deliberate and partly unplanned. Markides (1999): strategic management is planned and emergent, dynamic and interactive. Isenberg (1984): executives often sensed what to do before they could say why. Bolisani and Bratianu (2017): an integrated view joining rational planning with emergent planning. Mintzberg (1973): managers prefer live, concrete situations.
numbers: Kotter 1982 studied 15 executives; PIMS ran 19 years; Collins and Porras 6 years on 19 companies (as listed on the page, not verified).
limits: Secondary. Numbers are only study sizes.
agent_relevance: The integrated view (both) is the base case the scaffold should adopt; pure forms are not the aim.

source: Wikipedia 'Strategy' (opened): Mintzberg 1978 definition and five definitions
finding: 1978: strategy as 'a pattern in a stream of decisions'. Later five complementary definitions: plan, pattern, position, ploy, perspective. Plan is a directed course of action to reach intended goals; pattern is consistent past behaviour realized over time.
numbers: 5 definitions. The page attributes them to 1998 Strategy Safari; the five Ps are 1987 in the primary literature.
limits: Secondary; date mismatch noted.
agent_relevance: Plan versus pattern is the same contrast as our intended path versus executed trace.

source: Wikipedia 'Honda Super Cub' (opened): US entry 1959-1964, Boise dealer
finding: The best-known test case for emergence. American Honda was founded 1959 for service and parts. In 1960 a Boise, Idaho dealer sold more Honda 50s than all six Los Angeles dealers combined, after adding knobby tires and a bigger rear sprocket to sell it as a trail bike; that led to the Trail 50 in 1961. The 'nicest people' campaign began June 1963 and ran about 12 years. A textbook calls the case 'probably the best known and most debated case in business strategy'.
numbers: 1 dealer vs 6 dealers; 1960; 1961; June 1963; about 12 years.
limits: The page does not mention Pascale's 1984 account or the BCG 1975 report, so the planned-vs-emergent debate is not shown here. Single case, told after the fact.
agent_relevance: Shows the pattern: a cheap side probe found the winning use. Argues for keeping probe budget in S9 and for logging unexpected successes.

source: Pascale (1984) Perspectives on strategy: the real story behind Honda's success, California Management Review (recalled, not opened)
finding: Recalled: Pascale's interviews with the Honda US team said the entry plan targeted large bikes and the small Super Cub success came by accident, which became the standard example of emergent strategy. A competing account (Goold, 1996 in the same journal, by recollection) says Honda had a deliberate small-bike low-cost logic and that the 1975 BCG report oversold rational planning. Details not verified.
numbers: No verified figures.
limits: Memory only; no URL for the paper itself was opened. Contested: the two accounts disagree on facts. Do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Warning that the best-known emergence case is itself disputed. Good reason to log what actually happened, not tell the story afterwards.

source: Sarasvathy (2001) Causation and effectuation, AMR 26(2):243-263 (metadata via Crossref) plus Wikipedia 'Effectuation' (opened)
finding: Model of acting under uncertainty. Experienced founders asked to reason through a hypothetical venture paid less attention to predictive information, focused on limiting loss, and built partnerships. This is the entrepreneurship counterpart of emergent strategy: start from means at hand, not from a goal.
numbers: Crossref: 13,617 citing works. Wikipedia: 680 journal articles 2001-2024, review of 101 articles, five principles. Study N not on the page.
limits: The Wikipedia page lacked the sample size; do not state one. Think-aloud with a hypothetical task.
agent_relevance: A named alternative to goal-first planning for low-information tasks: start with what the agent can verify, expand by checks. Parallel to code-checked steps.

source: Yao et al. (2022) ReAct: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models, arXiv 2210.03629
finding: Interleaving a thought with each action (a reactive, emergent style) beats acting without thoughts, and complements pure chain-of-thought. ReAct failures differ: reasoning error 47% and search error 23% of 200 sampled HotpotQA trajectories; CoT failures are mainly hallucination (56%).
numbers: PaLM-540B. HotpotQA EM: Standard 28.7, CoT 29.4, Act 25.7, ReAct 27.4, ReAct to CoT-SC 35.1. FEVER: CoT 56.3, Act 58.9, ReAct 60.9, CoT-SC to ReAct 64.6. ALFWorld 134 games: ReAct best of 6 71%, average 57%, Act 45%, BUTLER 37%. WebShop success: ReAct 40.0, Act 30.1, human expert 59.6.
limits: ReAct is below CoT on HotpotQA (27.4 vs 29.4). Gains rest on few-shot examples. Not a business-strategy test; a stand-in for an emergent policy.
agent_relevance: Hybrid beats pure forms (ReAct plus CoT-SC best on HotpotQA 35.1), which mirrors the continuum view. Repeated steps are a ReAct failure signal that code can detect.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve prompting, arXiv 2305.04091
finding: Asking the model to first devise a plan and then carry it out (plan before execution, in one prompt) lifts zero-shot reasoning over plain chain-of-thought. Gains are mostly on arithmetic. Missing-step errors fall from 12% to 7% of sampled GSM8K errors; semantic errors do not move (27%).
numbers: text-davinci-003. Arithmetic average accuracy: zero-shot CoT 70.4, PS 72.9, PS+ 76.7, few-shot manual CoT 77.6. GSM8K: CoT 56.4, PS+ 59.3; with self-consistency PS+ 73.7 vs CoT 70.7. StrategyQA: manual CoT 71.2, zero-shot CoT 63.8, PS+ 65.4. CSQA: 78.3, 65.2, 71.9. Error sample N=100 on GSM8K.
limits: The plan is inside one prompt, not a separate stage with replanning. On commonsense tasks PS+ stays below few-shot CoT.
agent_relevance: A short up-front plan cuts omitted steps but not misunderstanding. The plan helps coverage, not meaning, so keep restate-the-problem as a separate step.

source: Prasad et al. (2023) ADaPT: as-needed decomposition and planning with language models, arXiv 2311.05772 (author list from memory)
finding: Decompose only when execution fails (as needed), recursively. This is plan on demand versus plan up front. Plan-and-Execute (fixed plan) equals ReAct on ALFWorld, does worse than ReAct on WebShop, and better on TextCraft; as-needed decomposition beats all of them.
numbers: GPT-3.5 test splits, success %. ALFWorld: ReAct 43.3, Plan-and-Execute 43.3, Reflexion 57.5, ADaPT 71.6. WebShop: ReAct 32.0, Plan-and-Execute 17.0, LATS 38.0, ADaPT 44.0. TextCraft: ReAct 19.0, Plan-and-Execute 27.0, Reflexion 32.0, ADaPT 52.0. TextCraft recipe depth 3: ReAct 1.8 vs ADaPT 38.7 (average depth 2.8); depth 2: 26.9 vs 78.2.
limits: Single model family. Per-depth gains read from tables, not figures. Authors are named from memory.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for the S9 design: plan finer only where the agent failed. The fixed-plan risk shows on WebShop (17 vs 32).

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning, arXiv 2303.11366
finding: A learning loop across trials: reflect on a failure, store the note, retry. Gains are large where the feedback is a real check (tests) and absent where feedback is vague. The paper reports no significant WebShop gain over ReAct.
numbers: ALFWorld 134 tasks: 130 solved in 12 trials; ReAct alone stalled between trials 6 and 7 at a 22% hallucination rate. HotpotQA 100 questions: Reflexion 0.80 vs 0.68 (CoT GT + GPT-4). HumanEval Python pass@1 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1. Rust 68.0 vs 60.0. MBPP Python 77.1 vs 80.1 (worse). LeetcodeHard 15.0 vs 7.5. False-positive rate MBPP 16.3% vs HumanEval 1.4%. Rust ablation: no tests 0.52, no reflection 0.60, full 0.68. Small model starchat-beta: 0.26 for both, no gain.
limits: Needs a strong model and a trustworthy check; stores only 1 to 3 experiences; can get stuck in local minima.
agent_relevance: Matches G2 and G3: revise only from real output and use a held-out check. The MBPP false positives show what happens when the check is weak.

source: Erdogan et al. (2025) Plan-and-Act: improving planning of agents for long-horizon tasks, arXiv 2503.09572 (authors from memory)
finding: Splits a planner (high-level steps) from an executor and lets the planner replan after each executor step. Replanning is the largest architectural gain. The closest published test of planned versus adaptive within one agent.
numbers: WebArena-Lite success: no planner 9.85%, base planner 14.21%, static planner with synthetic-data executor 43.63%, plus dynamic replanning 53.94% (+10.31 points), plus chain of thought 57.58%. Prior best WebRL-3.1-70B 49.1%. WebArena full 45.7% (Llama-70B), WebVoyager 81.36%. Executor tuning without a planner: 36.36% to 36.97%.
limits: The text has internal mismatches (CoT gain stated 4.36 vs table 3.64; intro and abstract quote different headline numbers). Trained on synthetic data; web tasks only.
agent_relevance: Replanning each step beat a static plan by 10 points. But replanning every step is a schedule, which conflicts with G1 unless gated by a signal. Test gated vs every-step replanning.

source: Csaszar, Ketkar and Kim (2024) Artificial intelligence and strategic decision-making: evidence from entrepreneurs and investors, arXiv 2408.08811
finding: A field-style test of LLMs on strategy work (business plans). LLM-generated plans were rated slightly above entrepreneurs' plans. LLM scores for startup plans track venture-investor scores. Frames strategy as search, representation and aggregation.
numbers: Generation: 309 plans from a European accelerator, 10 selected (5 accepted, 5 rejected), 250 US investors, 2,500 evaluations. LLM plans +0.14 SD (p<0.001), +5 points accept (p=0.003), +3 points invest (p=0.007), +2.55 on a 0-100 scale. Gain vs rejected plans +7/+8/+6 points, vanished vs accepted. Evaluation: 731 plans, 138 text-only analysed, 541 evaluations by 137 judges. LLM-VC correlation 0.52, R2 0.29, ICC 0.51 vs 0.25 between VCs. By criterion 0.21 (innovation) to 0.57 (financials).
limits: The paper does not discuss emergent versus planned strategy. Only 10 plans in the generation arm. Ratings, not realized firm outcomes. Weak on innovation (0.21).
agent_relevance: LLMs are fair at writing and scoring plans, but the paper gives no evidence they adapt a plan after contact with the world, which is the S9 question.

source: Csaszar et al. (2024) framework: search, representation, aggregation (arXiv 2408.08811, same paper)
finding: Formal vocabulary from the Carnegie school: search is trial until good enough on a performance landscape; representation is a simple model of the problem used to devise a solution; aggregation combines weak solutions by voting or specialisation. Planning corresponds to representation-led formation and emergence to search-led (my mapping).
numbers: No numbers for the framework.
limits: The mapping to planned vs emergent is my own reading; the paper never makes the contrast.
agent_relevance: Maps onto our states: restate problem = representation, operators = search, vote in code = aggregation. A ready way to ask which of the three S9 should adjust.

source: Kader and Lee (2024-2025) The emergence of strategic reasoning of large language models, arXiv 2412.13013
finding: Tests LLM strategic reasoning in three games, not firm strategy. Reasoning models show deeper level-k reasoning than standard ones, often at or above human level. Relevance is limited: 'strategic' here means other-player modelling, not plan formation.
numbers: 100 responses per model per condition. p-beauty contest (p=2/3, n=11) CH tau: GPT-o1 4.42, Claude-4-Sonnet-Thinking 4.00, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 2.87, GPT-4 2.39, Gemini 1.5 Flash 0.86. Guessing game: GPT-o1 2.84 vs humans 1.78 (N=88 in the human data). 11-20 money request: humans 3.14 vs GPT-o1 1.21.
limits: Different meaning of 'strategic'. Humans beaten in some games and not in others. Human data come from other studies.
agent_relevance: Warns against reading game-theory benchmarks as a test of planning versus emergence. Use plan-execution benchmarks instead.

source: Levinthal (1997), Gavetti and Levinthal (2000), March (1991): computational models of search (recalled, not opened)
finding: Recalled: NK landscape simulations treat strategy as local search (emergent, experience-driven) versus cognitive search with a simplified map of the landscape (planned, forward-looking). Gavetti and Levinthal 2000 combined both: a forward-looking representation narrows the region, local experience refines it. March 1991 framed exploration versus exploitation. Exact results not verified.
numbers: No verified figures.
limits: Memory only. Simulation, not field data. Results depend on landscape ruggedness.
agent_relevance: Evidence-by-model that both are needed: a rough map first, local search second. Fits a two-phase scaffold.

source: Quinn (1978, 1980) logical incrementalism and Lindblom (1959) muddling through (recalled, not opened)
finding: Recalled: Lindblom argued that policy is made by successive limited comparisons, not comprehensive rational analysis. Quinn studied large firms through interviews and said executives build strategy step by step with a broad direction, which he called logical incrementalism. Both pre-date Mintzberg's emergent concept. Wikipedia 'Strategic management' lists both only as references.
numbers: No verified numbers; the Quinn sample of about 10 large firms is from memory.
limits: Memory only.
agent_relevance: Precedent for small, checked steps with a stated direction, close to the scaffold's loop of attempt, check, revise.

source: Brews and Hunt (1999) Learning to plan and planning to learn, SMJ 20 (recalled, not opened)
finding: Recalled: tested the planning school against the learning school with survey data; found that formal planning and incremental learning are not opposed, and that planning with flexibility did well in unstable environments. Sample and effect sizes not verified.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Memory only.
agent_relevance: Supports a combined design but needs verification before it is used as evidence.

source: Wikipedia 'Igor Ansoff' (opened): the planning-school founder
finding: Ansoff is the father figure of formal strategic planning. Corporate Strategy (1965) was an immediate success; he joined Lockheed corporate planning in 1957, was professor at Carnegie Mellon 1963-1968 and founding dean at Vanderbilt's Owen school 1969-1973; later work on environmental turbulence and real-time strategic management. The page does not cover the Mintzberg debate.
limits: The page carries single-source and reliability tags.
agent_relevance: Ansoff's turbulence idea is the planning side's answer: the more turbulent the setting, the more real-time adaptation. A task-type moderator to measure for our agent.
